title: How to read cross-stitch chart symbols
subtitle: Understanding the symbol key and navigating a counted chart
excerpt: A cross-stitch chart is a grid in which each filled square represents one complete cross-stitch. The colour of each stitch is shown by a symbol inside the square, and the chart includes a key that matches every symbol to a thread colour number. Reading a chart accurately is the foundation of counted cross-stitch.
sourceNotes: Chart reading for counted cross-stitch. Standard guidance in major cross-stitch publisher guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads.
The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch.

content.text: A cross-stitch chart shows the design as a grid where each filled square is one complete stitch. Each square carries a symbol, and a key at the side of the chart links every symbol to a
colour number. The chart squares correspond directly to the squares of the
: one chart square equals one stitch over one Aida square.

Locate the symbol key before beginning. The key lists every symbol used in the chart alongside the corresponding thread colour number (commonly DMC or Anchor). Match each symbol visually to what appears in the chart squares.

Find the centre of the chart, usually marked with arrows on the chart margins. Find the centre of the fabric by folding it in half vertically, then horizontally. Mark the centre of the fabric with a small basting stitch in a contrasting thread. The chart centre and fabric centre should align when you begin stitching.

Work outward from the centre of the design rather than from a corner. Starting at the centre keeps the design correctly positioned on the fabric regardless of where the stitching ends up relative to the fabric edges.

As you stitch each area, mark the corresponding squares on a photocopy or printout of the chart with a pencil or light highlighter. This prevents losing your place when you set the project down and resume later. The chart should be clear and readable at all times.

Check your position on the chart against the fabric every 10-15 stitches. Count back to a completed area you are certain of, rather than counting forward from your last stitch. Counting backwards from a verified point catches miscounts before they travel far.

items.symptom: The design appears off-centre on the fabric
items.cause: The fabric centre was not correctly found, or the first stitch was placed incorrectly on the chart.
items.fix: Count back from the stitches already done to the design centre, then count the same number of squares on the chart to verify the starting position. If there is an offset, note how many squares and rows by, and adjust the remaining stitching to compensate.

items.symptom: A whole section is one row off compared to the chart
items.cause: A miscounted row early in the design has shifted all stitches above it by one position.
items.fix: Identify exactly where the shift occurred by counting down from a known correct area. Unpick only from that row forward, correct the position, and restitch.

content.text: Printing the chart on paper rather than reading from a screen makes chart-reading considerably easier. The paper can be annotated as you go, and held alongside the fabric without the screen timing out. Some stitchers use a magnetic chart-keeper with a line guide to track their position row by row.
